text: During pre‑training, REALM rebuilds the MIPS document index about once every 500 training steps, i.e., it performs one index refresh for roughly every 500 steps of retriever training【1】.
MonoBERT truncates the query to a maximum length of 64 tokens before feeding it to BERT [1].

When DPR is trained with in‑batch negatives, adding hard negatives that are retrieved by a keyword‑based BM25 search still provides a benefit: using a single BM25 hard negative per batch improves performance noticeably, while adding more than one yields little additional gain【5】. The authors’ best‑performing model therefore combines in‑batch gold negatives with one BM25 hard negative per batch【8】.

Fusion‑in‑Decoder first encodes each retrieved passage (and its title) separately, then concatenates the resulting passage representations and lets the decoder attend to all of them jointly, so the evidence is fused only in the decoder stage【4】.  
RAG, by contrast, integrates retrieval directly into the generation model: a dense retriever provides a set of documents that the generator attends to together, without a separate re‑ranking or extractive reader, and the model marginalizes over all retrieved documents during generation【3】.  

Thus, Fusion‑in‑Decoder performs independent encoding followed by decoder‑only fusion, whereas RAG performs end‑to‑end retrieval‑augmented generation with joint attention over the retrieved passages.

Across the BEIR zero‑shot benchmark, DPR does not consistently beat BM25. In the BEIR results table, DPR’s nDCG@10 scores are lower than BM25 on several datasets (e.g., 0.177 vs. 0.228 on MS MARCO, 0.332 vs. 0.656 on TREC‑COVID, 0.127 vs. 0.465 on BioASQ) and only surpass BM25 on a few (e.g., 0.388 vs. 0.296 on MS MARCO, 0.654 vs. 0.406 on TREC‑COVID) [1]. The BEIR analysis further notes that many approaches that outperform BM25 in‑domain perform poorly in zero‑shot settings, highlighting that strong in‑domain gains do not guarantee out‑of‑domain superiority [4]. Thus, the large win DPR shows on open‑domain QA does not uniformly extend to zero‑shot BEIR datasets.

The experiments showed that learned (trainable) positional embeddings performed almost the same as the original sinusoidal embeddings, so the trainable vectors did not achieve noticeably higher accuracy [2]. The authors kept the fixed sine‑cosine version because it is hypothesized to let the model extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training [2].
FlashAttention enabled a Transformer to achieve better‑than‑chance performance for the first time on the Path‑X long‑range benchmark, using a sequence length of 16 K tokens【4】【5】.

The authors filtered out any page that contained placeholder text (e.g., the phrase “lorem ipsum”) and also removed any page that contained source‑code indicators such as a curly‑brace “{”, which is common in programming languages【1】.

ELECTRA keeps the two networks tied only on their embedding matrices: the token embeddings (and, when a small generator is used, also the positional embeddings) are shared between generator and discriminator, while all other encoder weights remain separate【1】.

BERT first pre‑trains using a short sequence length of 128 for the majority of the training, and then switches to the full length of 512 for the remaining portion. Specifically, 128‑token sequences are used for 90 % of the pre‑training steps, and 512‑token sequences are used for the final 10 % of steps [1].

The original BERT paper reported that removing the next‑sentence prediction (NSP) loss harms performance, causing notable degradation on tasks such as QNLI, MNLI and SQuAD 1.1【5】.  
In contrast, the RoBERTa study found that training without the NSP loss matches or slightly improves downstream task performance, and that the NSP objective is not necessary for strong results【6】.

ELECTRA’s discriminator is trained to predict whether each token in the input has been replaced, so its loss is computed over **all** input positions rather than only the masked subset used by BERT’s MLM objective【1†L1-L4】【2†L1-L4】. Because the model receives a supervisory signal from every token, it can extract useful training information from many more tokens per training step. This broader learning signal lets ELECTRA converge more quickly—training “much faster than BERT”—and, when fully trained, achieve higher downstream accuracy for a given amount of compute【6†L1-L4】【7†L1-L4】.

The passages do not support the claim that ELECTRA works best when the generator is larger than the discriminator; in fact, they report that models perform best when the generator is only ¼–½ the size of the discriminator, because a too‑strong generator makes the discrimination task overly difficult and forces the discriminator to allocate many of its parameters to modeling the generator rather than the true data distribution【1】. Thus, the context provides no evidence for the premise that a larger generator yields better performance.
The FLAN authors manually wrote ten instruction templates for each dataset [1][3][6].

If the instruction‑tuning mixture contains no chain‑of‑thought (CoT) examples, the model’s ability to perform step‑by‑step reasoning gets worse—indeed, instruction finetuning without any CoT data actually degrades reasoning performance compared to the baseline [1].

The RL stage uses chain‑of‑thought (CoT) prompting to generate preference labels, but the CoT reasoning often forces the feedback model to assign near‑certain probabilities (close to 0 or 1), which are poorly calibrated for reinforcement learning. To avoid these overly extreme targets, the authors clamp the CoT‑derived probabilities to a moderate interval, improving robustness and behavior of the RL‑CAI model. The clamping is set to keep probabilities within roughly 40 %–60 % [5][8].

DPO’s summarization quality remains relatively stable as the decoding temperature increases, whereas PPO’s quality drops sharply. In the TL;DR experiments DPO achieved about a 61 % win rate at temperature 0.0 and stayed robust across higher temperatures, while PPO’s best win rate (≈57 %) was only reached at temperature 0.0 and degraded to the level of the base GPT‑J model when the temperature was raised [1]. This indicates that DPO is much more tolerant of temperature changes than PPO.

InstructGPT first fits a reward model to human‑generated preference data and then uses reinforcement learning (typically PPO) to train a policy that maximizes the learned reward while staying close to the original model [2][3]. In contrast, Direct Preference Optimization bypasses both an explicit reward model and any reinforcement‑learning loop; it rewrites the RLHF objective as a binary‑cross‑entropy loss that directly updates the language‑model policy to increase the log‑probability of preferred responses relative to dispreferred ones [1][4][6]. Thus, InstructGPT relies on a two‑stage RLHF pipeline, whereas DPO turns the preference data into a single‑step, RL‑free optimization.

Adapter modules are added to a frozen pre‑trained network with their parameters set so that the module initially behaves like an identity function.  In practice the two projection layers inside the bottleneck are initialized to near‑zero values (or, equivalently, the whole adapter is initialized to a near‑identity mapping) so that the original network’s behavior is unchanged at the start of training [1][5].  This near‑identity initialization is required for stable training; if the adapters start far from the identity, the model may fail to train or the original network’s representations can be disrupted early on [1][5].

Directly updating the prefix parameters $P_{\theta}$ is unstable and can even hurt performance, so the method re‑parameterizes the prefix: a smaller matrix $P'_{\theta}$ is learned and then passed through a feed‑forward network $\textsc{MLP}_{\theta}$ to produce the actual prefix $P_{\theta}$, after which the re‑parameterization weights can be discarded and only $P_{\theta}$ is kept [3].

Double Quantization is a two‑stage quantization process in which the quantization constants produced by the first (4‑bit) quantization are themselves quantized a second time. The first‑stage constants \(c_{2}^{\text{FP32}}\) are treated as inputs to a second quantizer that stores them as 8‑bit floating‑point values \(c_{2}^{\text{FP8}}\) together with a new set of higher‑precision constants \(c_{1}^{\text{FP32}}\) [1]. By compressing these constants, Double Quantization reduces the memory overhead that quantization constants normally add to a model—approximately 0.5 bits per parameter when using a blocksize of 64—down to about 0.127 bits per parameter, saving roughly 0.37 bits per parameter (≈3 GB for a 65 B model) [1][3].

The authors first trained a model on the full set of ≈ 1.3 billion noisy text pairs and then used that model to rank each pair against a pool of one million random passages; a pair was retained only if it appeared in the top‑k (k = 2) ranked list, i.e., the model’s prediction was consistent with the label【1†L9-L13】. After applying this consistency‑based filter, about 270 million text pairs remained for contrastive pre‑training【1†L13-L15】.
The MTEB benchmark showed that SimCSE performs poorly on clustering and retrieval tasks, even though it achieves strong results on semantic‑textual‑similarity benchmarks【1】.

Adapters insert separate adapter layers into each Transformer block, typically one or two per block, which are processed sequentially after the original layers [2]. Because these extra layers must be executed during the forward pass, they add measurable inference latency, especially in online settings with batch size 1 [1][2].  

LoRA, by contrast, injects trainable low‑rank matrices (the factorized \(L_{1}\) and \(L_{2}\) projections) in parallel to the existing weight matrices (e.g., \(W_{q}\) and \(W_{v}\)) of the frozen model [3][5][8]. Since the LoRA matrices are merged with the frozen weights at deployment, they do not introduce any additional inference latency compared with a fully fine‑tuned model [3][8].

LoRA’s memory footprint is tiny compared with the full model: for a 7 B LLaMA model the LoRA parameters occupy only about 26 MB, while the 4‑bit base model itself uses roughly 5 048 MB of memory [3].  

QLoRA’s headline result shows a far larger reduction: finetuning a 65 B‑parameter model normally requires more than 780 GB of GPU memory, but QLoRA brings this down to under 48 GB, saving on the order of 730 GB of memory [2]. Additionally, QLoRA’s double‑quantization saves about 0.37 bits per parameter, which corresponds to roughly 3 GB saved for a 65 B model [4].

Prompting the model to output a sequence of filler dots (the “variable compute only” ablation) performed roughly the same as the baseline and did not improve performance, indicating that this substitution did not help. [1][7]

A ReAct agent can issue Wikipedia‑search actions (e.g., “search x” or “look up x”) that cause the model to receive the retrieved passage as an observation, which it can then reason over for HotpotQA and FEVER [5][1]

DeepSeek‑R1’s reinforcement‑learning stages add a “language‑consistency” reward that measures how many words in the chain‑of‑thought belong to the target language and adds this proportion to the overall reward, thereby penalizing reasoning traces that switch between languages【8】. The authors note that this extra reward makes the output more readable and aligned with human preferences, but it also leads to a modest drop in overall model performance【8】.

Toolformer teaches a language model to use external tools by finetuning it on a large number of sampled API calls that are filtered to keep only those that reduce the loss on subsequent tokens, and then interleaving the retained calls with the original text so the model learns when and how to invoke tools such as calculators, search engines, or translators in a self‑supervised manner without human annotations [4][3][5]. The approach generates potential API calls from a few human‑written examples, uses a self‑supervised loss to identify useful calls, and fine‑tunes the model on this filtered data, enabling it to decide autonomously which tool to use and when to use it [6]. The context does not provide information on how ReAct teaches tool use.
